title: DESSLib–Benchmark instances for optimization of decentralized energy supply systems
contribution: Problem statement of the DESSLib benchmark: superstructure-based synthesis of decentralized energy supply systems (which units, what size, what operation per load case) as a nonlinear model maximizing net present value, written for a public instance library built from real-world data.
problem_entry: An application: energy costs of chemical parks, districts and hospitals match the companies' profits in magnitude, and structure, dimension and operation influence each other, so they must be optimized together (p. 1).
key_idea: A superstructure fixes the maximum number of boilers, CHP engines, turbo and absorption chillers; continuous sizes within bounds, part-load operation per load case and a net present value objective; functions and parameters are deferred to the companion document S081 (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Nonlinear investment-cost, part-load and CHP electricity functions (an MINLP, not a MILP); quasi-stationary behaviour, no start-up time, no storage; demands met with equality; several units of one type allowed, unlike classical process synthesis (pp. 2-3).
positioning: Cites Frangopoulos et al. for the three decision levels, Voll et al. 2013, Voll's thesis and the submitted MINLP paper for DESS synthesis, and Farkas et al. for the contrast with classical process synthesis (pp. 1-2, 4).
writing: A three-page technical note: motivation, the three decision levels as a numbered list, the model in prose with symbols, details deferred to the companion document and the website (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated (pp. 1-3).

method_links.note: Test-set side, co-authored: a public benchmark library from real-world data, the 'real or public' instances of the taste quick-check, with its problem statement released as a document of its own (taste G2). How hard the instances are and which methods were tested on them is not stated here.

transferable: Release an application benchmark as two short, cross-referenced documents, the problem statement and the instance structure with every component parameter, next to the instance files on a website (p. 3; S081 p. 1).
coauthors: Björn Bahl, Sebastian Goderbauer, Fritz Arnold, Philip Voll, André Bardow, Arie M.C.A. Koster (Lübbecke fifth of seven)

quotes.text: However, the levels influence each other, thus only a simultaneous optimization will find a global optimal solution.
Note that an optimal DESS is likely to contain multiple components of one type which is in strong contrast to classical process synthesis problems

title: DESSLib–Benchmark Instance Structure, Component Models and Parameters
contribution: Data document of DESSLib: naming, structure and generation of the instances (superstructure size by number of load cases, ten demand-perturbed replicates per class, peak load cases of zero duration) and all unit parameters and nonlinear part-load and investment-cost functions.
problem_entry: A documentation need: the name convention, structure and generation of the instances and every parameter and function of the component models, the problem itself being described in S055 (abstract, p. 1).
key_idea: One real-world case condensed into representative load cases plus zero-duration peak cases; instances named by superstructure size (spread evenly over four unit types) and number of load cases; ten replicates per class with demands randomly varied by a small factor (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Tables of size ranges, efficiencies, maintenance and minimum part-load factors and economic parameters; quadratic part-load expressions and fractional-power investment curves; part-load behaviour assumed independent of unit size; the size of the random factor is not given (pp. 1-4).
positioning: Builds on the real-world example of Voll et al. 2013 and takes component data from measured CHP data (ASUE), Fabrizio's thesis, turbo-chiller manufacturers, the IUTA price atlas and industrial partners (pp. 1, 3, 5).
writing: A data sheet: naming convention with an example file name, the file layout as a three-part list, parameter tables and numbered functions with their coefficients (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated (pp. 1-4).

method_links.note: Step 2, test-set design, co-authored: difficulty laid out along two named size dimensions with ten structurally identical, numerically perturbed replicates per class, and every parameter published so the set can be regenerated.

transferable: Build an instance family from one real data set: condense the time series into representative load cases, add each peak as a load case of zero duration so the design is feasible for all observed demands, and name every file by its size parameters (p. 1).
Per structural class, generate replicates that differ only in perturbed data values (ten per class), so a method can be judged per class across data variation (pp. 1-2).
coauthors: Björn Bahl, Sebastian Goderbauer, Fritz Arnold, Philip Voll, André Bardow, Arie M.C.A. Koster (Lübbecke fifth of seven)

quotes.text: Note that peak load cases have a duration of zero.
Within each S/L-category, the absolute values of the energy demands are randomly varied by a small factor.

title: A Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for Packing Cuts in Undirected Graphs
contribution: First exact algorithm and computational study for cut packing: branch-price-and-cut on the Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of a replicated min-cut model, with min-cut and binary-program pricing, branching on aggregated original variables and then on edge pairs, clique cuts and an edge-clique-cover bound, which solves graphs with up to several hundred vertices and beats the compact model in SCIP and in GCG.
problem_entry: No computational record for an NP-hard, W[1]-hard problem with applications ('So far it could not be solved exactly'), plus the question how complexity results match computational experience (abstract p. 1; pp. 2-3).
key_idea: The extended set-packing model over all cuts derived as the Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of n-1 replicated min-cut models with identical subproblems aggregated; combinatorial min-cut pricing at the root, binary-program pricing after branching, a disjoint-column heuristic and a column pool, branching on aggregated original edge variables then Ryan-Foster, clique cuts and an edge-clique-cover upper bound added before column generation (pp. 2-10).
assumptions: Connected undirected graphs with nontrivial shores; about 100 instances: random graphs (Rudy, Randgraph, NetworkX, seed 1), MUSKETEER copies, DIMACS graphs with at most 500 vertices, Trick's coloring graphs with fewer than 5,000 edges; BHOSLIB tried and dropped (pp. 1, 10-12).
proof_devices: NP-completeness of pricing with diff-branching constraints by reduction from independent set (Theorem 3.1, p. 7)
W[1]-hardness of k-cut packing from Colbourn's NP-hardness construction (Corollary 2.1, p. 3)
Clique example: LP bound n/2 against optimum 1, motivating clique inequalities (p. 8)
Dominance: a cut with a disconnected shore is never in an optimal LP solution, so it is split into its components (p. 6)
A same-branch cut that cannot be split is added anyway, slowing but not harming the search (pp. 7-8)
Odd-cycle duals change only the pricing objective, so the combinatorial pricer stays valid at the root (p. 9)
experiments: SCIP 3.0.1 with CPLEX 12.4.0.1, i7-2600, 3,600 s; on 12 Randgraph instances the compact model solved 3 in SCIP and 5 in GCG 2.0.1, the basic tailored code 8 and the full code 12; Table I with shifted geometric means but no shift; 5 of 9 DIMACS graphs solved against 1 of 9 matched random graphs; three-way ablation profiles; random graphs above 40 vertices and all BHOSLIB root nodes unsolved (pp. 10-14).
positioning: Places cut packing in duality theory (Fulkerson, Robacker) and complexity (Colbourn, Caprara et al.); takes the extended model from Caprara et al. 2004 and disjoint columns from Desrochers et al. 1992; GCG is the generic alternative it is measured against (pp. 1-3, 6, 11, 14).
writing: A first-person-plural contribution paragraph ('We are not aware of any experimental results'), hedged readings of the results, and a conclusion that ends in a verdict and two concrete research questions (pp. 2, 13-14).
limits_future: Size limits stated as 80 vertices on random graphs, 500 on partitioning graphs and 5,000 edges on coloring graphs, although p. 12 reports failures above 40 vertices on random graphs; future: better edge clique covers and other IP or semidefinite min-cut formulations for pricing (pp. 12, 14).

method_links.note: Steps 1, 2, 5, 6: compact model first, extended model derived as its Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation; compact model run in SCIP 3.0.1 and in GCG 2.0.1 on the same machine and limit as the tailored code; built on SCIP; aggregated original variables branched on first.

Dating of the increment: already in 2016 (preliminary version 2014) GCG is a competitor rather than a probe, and the paper concludes that a problem-specific implementation still considerably pays while generic solvers may become competitive soon; no probe step precedes the build.

Steps 1, 3, 5: random sets beside literature graphs, each real graph paired with a same-size random graph and a MUSKETEER-edited copy; the gap to GCG explained (same pricing problem, other branching rules); three-way ablation; failures printed (BHOSLIB, random graphs above 40 vertices).

Steps 5-6: shifted geometric means without the shift; one generator seed; the conclusion's 80-vertex limit against the failures above 40 vertices in section 4.2; 'almost every instance' before the counts are given.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The study tests whether complexity and approximation results show in computation: the classes solvable in polynomial time (bipartite, chordal) also run faster in the exponential-time algorithm, and the factor-2 gap between alpha(G) and gamma(G) does not appear; matching theory with computational experience is an aim stated in the abstract.

transferable: Derive the extended formulation as the Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of a replicated compact model and aggregate the identical subproblems, which removes the replication symmetry; branch first on the aggregated original variables (the sum of the edge variables over all copies) (pp. 2-3, 6).

When branching breaks the combinatorial pricer (negative duals), switch to a binary-program pricer only in the nodes that need it, and prove the branched pricing problem hard to justify the switch (pp. 4-7).
Split any priced column whose shore is disconnected into its components and add those; the original column cannot be in an optimal LP solution (p. 6).
Compute a combinatorial upper bound (an edge clique cover) before column generation and put its clique inequalities into the master from the start (p. 10).
Ablate in three directions: disable each component in the full code, enable each in the basic code, and disable several together (pp. 13-14).
For each real instance, add a random graph of the same size and a structure-preserving edited copy (MUSKETEER), to tell structure effects from size effects (p. 12).
coauthors: Martin Bergner, Jonas T. Witt (alphabetical author list)

quotes.text: In our case, the combinatorial pricing is a nice add-on but nonetheless has not that much influence on the solution time as expected.
We conclude that at the current state of the art, it still considerably pays to consider a problem-specific implementation, even though generic solvers may become competitive soon.

title: Optimization of the reconfiguration planning of handling systems based on parallel manipulators with Delta-like architecture
contribution: Selects p Delta-robot configurations out of 2,250 and assigns 200 handling tasks to them with a p-median model whose energy costs come from inverse dynamics, showing an 11.8% energy saving over a line of identical robots in one case study.
problem_entry: Reconfigurable Delta robots offer many dimensional and functional configurations; choose p of them and assign known handling tasks so that energy is minimal (abstract p. 1; pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Model selection and assignment as a p-median problem, with energy costs from inverse dynamics (Kane's equations for frame-mounted extensions) precomputed for all 450,000 task-configuration pairs, then solve the standard IP with Gurobi (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Standard p-median IP; 200 tasks generated from market figures of more than 150 commercial Delta variants; 2,250 configurations from a fixed discretization; symmetric geometry, scaled masses, no braking energy recovered; no set-up times, costs or capacities (pp. 3-5).
proof_devices: p-median formulation of configuration selection and task allocation, infeasible pairs as penalty costs (eqs. 1-6, p. 4)
Cost matrix of 450,000 energy values precomputed by inverse dynamics, with Kane's equations for frame-mounted extensions (eqs. 10-11, p. 5)
Link masses scaled linearly and inertias by squared or cubed length ratios (eqs. 7-9, p. 5)
experiments: One instance (200 tasks, 2,250 configurations), Python and Gurobi, p = 6: 11.8% less energy than six copies of the best all-task configuration, 63.2% less than the worst, a plateau at 13.9% for p > 15; no solve times reported (pp. 5-6).
positioning: Reviews reconfiguration in robotics (modularity, static and dynamic reconfiguration, morphing, operation modes) and Delta variants in industry and patents, and takes p-median precedents from glass cutting, packaging sizes (including the first author's), an Amazon patent, cell formation and clustering (pp. 2-4).
writing: Engineering-journal structure (reconfiguration types, Delta variants, methodology, model, results, discussion and outlook); integer programming introduced for a robotics readership ('a so-called integer program'); the outlook mixes limits with extensions (pp. 2-7).
limits_future: Tasks from market figures and limited to 200, a fixed discretization, set-up and capacity ignored; future: real process data, a sensitivity analysis, column generation for larger configuration spaces, a capacitated p-median with opening costs (pp. 4-7).

method_links.note: Steps 1-3: the compact p-median is written and solved by a current commercial solver first; column generation is named only for the next step, when the configuration space and computing times grow. That configurations would become the columns is inferred; the text does not say.

Steps 1 and 6, taste B2: one generated instance whose tasks come from market statistics rather than an owner's process data, no solve times, yet 'novel and rigorous' and 'general applicability' are claimed from it; whose wording this is cannot be told from the text.

transferable: To choose k designs from a large discrete design space and assign jobs to them, write a p-median: designs as facilities, jobs as customers, infeasible pairs as penalty costs (pp. 3-4).
Precompute the full job-by-design cost matrix with the domain simulator once, give it to a standard p-median IP, and sweep p to show the saving curve (pp. 5-6).
Measure the saving against the natural no-reconfiguration baseline: p identical copies of the best, and of the worst, design that covers every job (p. 6).
coauthors: Jan Brinker (first author), Yukio Takeda, Burkhard Corves

quotes.text: At this stage, set-up times and costs as well as capacity and occupancy figures are not considered in order to demonstrate general feasibility of the approach.
The two latter aspects advocate for a different modeling and more elaborate solution technique known as column generation.

title: A strongly polynomial contraction-expansion algorithm for network flow problems
contribution: A generic contraction algorithm for capacitated minimum cost flow that contains MMCC and the primal network simplex as extreme cases, and a Contraction-Expansion variant that keeps MMCC's strongly polynomial O(m^3 n^2) bound while running faster than MMCC, but slower than Cancel-and-Tighten, on DIMACS instances.
problem_entry: The network simplex works well despite degenerate pivots while the strongly polynomial MMCC is no match in practice; the aim is to understand algorithms with strictly positive steps, not to beat leading codes, with column-generation oracles as a motive (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Contract the trees of a linearly independent arc set (the free arcs) into roots and price minimum mean cycles on the contracted network; P empty gives MMCC, P basic gives the network simplex; Contraction-Expansion shrinks P to the arcs free before and after each cancellation until a Type 3 cycle ends the phase (pp. 3-13).
assumptions: Capacitated minimum cost flow with bounds, balanced supplies and no multiarcs; a linearly independent hidden set, maintainable from nonbasic solutions; a basic initial phase solution and a cap of n cancellations before the full residual network in the complexity proof (pp. 2, 5, 14).
proof_devices: Telescoping: cost equals reduced cost on any cycle, directed or not (Proposition 1, p. 2)
Arc cost transfer: duals fixed along tree paths give hidden arcs zero reduced cost, so a contracted cycle's reduced cost equals its extended cost (Procedure 1, Proposition 4, pp. 6-7)
A normalized pricing LP whose extreme points are minimum mean cycles (Proposition 5, p. 7)
Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions when the hidden set lies in the free arcs, only sufficient otherwise (Proposition 6, p. 8)
Sandwich μ_H ≤ μ_G ≤ μ_H:G between contracted, true and extended mean costs (Proposition 10, p. 10)
Phases ended by a measurable jump of a lower bound (Type 3 cycle), with arc fixing restated on the lower bound (Definitions 3-4, Propositions 11-12, pp. 12-13)
A phase in O(m^2 n) via at most n + m cancellations, O(m^3 n^2) overall (Proposition 13, Theorem 1, pp. 13-14)
experiments: C++, i7-4770K at 3.50 GHz, 16 GB, Windows 10; DIMACS families, version A of GRIDGRAPH, NETGEN and GRIDGEN profiled; baselines MMCC and Cancel-and-Tighten: CE beats MMCC more as size grows (1,907 s against 15,629 s on gridgen_sr_13a) but CT is fastest (36 s); losses on ROAD (no contraction) and NETGEN printed; the largest instances excluded because MMCC was too slow; no time limit stated (pp. 15-17).
positioning: Continues Goldberg-Tarjan's MMCC, Radzik-Goldberg's phases and the authors' 2015 MMCC paper with Cancel-and-Tighten; adopts the nomenclature of Ahuja et al.; credits the network simplex and cost scaling (Kovács 2015) as the practical leaders (pp. 1-3, 10-11, 17).
writing: Constructive exposition with many small figures, propositions with short proofs and a behavioural study before the algorithm; the conclusion opens with a note to network simplex users and names its new concept ('The Type 3 cycle is born.') (pp. 1, 10, 17).
limits_future: The same O(m^3 n^2) bound as MMCC, not competitive, the practical leaders not compared, omitted families believed irrelevant; future: whether the expansion is necessary (conjectured) and strongly polynomial algorithms combined with practical observations (pp. 12, 17).

method_links.note: Step 6, with step 5's losses: the purpose is understanding, not beating leading codes, and the paper does not pretend to be competitive yet; the losses to CT, on ROAD and on NETGEN are printed with their mechanism, and the exclusion of the largest instances is explained.

Step 3: the baselines are the algorithm being generalized (MMCC) and its sibling (CT); the network simplex and cost scaling, called the practical leaders, are not run, and only version A of three families is profiled.

Exit B without enumeration: a behavioural study on one instance counts the exceptions to monotonicity (21 of 14,258 iterations; four of 7,294 cancellations for CT) and reads phases off the plots; the expansion scheme is designed from these readings and proved, and the open part is published as a conjecture. No option space is enumerated.
Known algorithms (MMCC, the primal network simplex) recast as the extreme cases of one construction: a synthesis inside a research article rather than a survey, in the first author's line.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one-parameter family with known algorithms as its extremes
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The contraction algorithm turns into MMCC with no hidden arcs and into the primal network simplex with the basic arcs hidden; the new Contraction-Expansion algorithm lives between them and controls the parameter during the run. Also in S044.

transferable: Hide the trees of free arcs by contraction and fix their duals along tree paths: hidden arcs get zero reduced cost, each contracted cycle's reduced cost equals its full cost, and a smaller pricing network certifies optimality (pp. 6-8).
For a phase-based complexity proof of an algorithm whose optimality parameter oscillates, end phases on a measurable jump of a lower bound and restate arc fixing on that bound (pp. 11-14).
Build the worst case of the proof into the code as a cap (at most n cancellations before switching to the full residual network), so the bound holds whatever the expansion does (p. 14).
Print the instance class where the method loses, with the mechanism: no free variables, hence no contraction, only overhead (p. 15).
coauthors: Jean Bertrand Gauthier (first and corresponding author), Jacques Desrosiers

quotes.text: We should also mention that the goal of this research is not to beat leading algorithms on network problems.
We therefore just get penalized with the contraction computational overhead.

title: Vector space decomposition for solving large-scale linear programs
contribution: Vector space decomposition, a primal LP framework in which one parameter (a subspace basis of basic columns) decides which duals pricing fixes and which it optimizes, unifying the primal simplex, IPS, DCA and minimum weighted cycle-canceling and characterizing the variants with positive steps and with interior directions.
problem_entry: Primal simplex degeneracy: Dantzig's rule has a 'visibility problem' about which basic variables can move, and column generation encodes the primal simplex in its pricing and inherits its degeneracy (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Choose a subspace basis A_P of basic columns; fix the duals of the rows tied to P and optimize the others to maximize the minimum normalized reduced cost; lift the projected cycle and step; P = B, F, a superset of F or the empty set gives the primal simplex, IPS, DCA or MWCC (pp. 5-10).
assumptions: Bounded LP with m < n, A of full row rank, feasible with a finite optimum; a basic feasible start; positive normalization weights, fixed or updated dynamically (pp. 2-3, 6, 8).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: the cost and the reduced cost of a cycle are equal (p. 4)
Optimality conditions on the residual problem (Proposition 1, after Gauthier et al. 2014, p. 4)
Row and column partition by T_P^-1, with compatibility as membership in the span of A_P (Definition 4, p. 5)
A positive step size whenever P lies in the free variables (Proposition 2, p. 9)
Interior directions as nonnegative combinations of edge directions, by Minkowski-Weyl (Proposition 3, p. 10)
The Klee-Minty polytope solved by MWCC in one iteration (p. 12)
experiments: none (illustrative examples on a three-variable LP and the Klee-Minty polytope; observations on MWCC and on pricing with original costs stated without numbers) (pp. 10-13).
positioning: Opens from Dantzig and Thapa's pivot-rule remark, contrasts steepest edge and Devex, unifies the Montréal methods (IPS, DCA, ISUD, positive edge) with Goldberg-Tarjan's cycle canceling, and cites Bixby 2002 for the strength of dual simplex and barrier (pp. 1-2, 9-13).
writing: Each concept introduced in its own subsection and then tied together; special cases summarized in a dated figure; explicit disclaimers on competitiveness and on direction quality; a conclusion that restates the contributions and lists research perspectives (pp. 2, 10-13).
limits_future: No claim of a competitive generic implementation, direction quality hard to judge, complexity transfer left for another paper; future: a cancel-and-tighten analogue for LPs, stabilization and dual-optimal inequalities in column generation, heuristic pricers with original costs (pp. 9, 11-13).

method_links.note: Step 2 inside a research article: published remedies for degeneracy (IPS, DCA, MWCC and the simplex itself) are put into one notation under one parameter and dated in one figure; not a survey, and the first author's line.

Step 6: the framework is said not to imply a competitive generic implementation, and the paper does not claim that one variant gives better directions, giving a modified example that reverses the effect.

Checkpoint on counts: two experimental claims come without numbers, the same slow behaviour observed for MWCC as for MMCC, and pricing with original costs 'already proving elegant in our recent experiments'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one-parameter family with known algorithms as its extremes
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: One parameter P gives the primal simplex (P = B), IPS (P = F), DCA (P a superset of F) and MWCC, MMCC on networks (P empty), dated in one figure; the two properties proved are read off the parameter. Also in S061.

transferable: Classify pricing rules by which duals they fix and which they optimize; fixing the duals of the nondegenerate basic variables (P = F) yields positive steps along edges (pp. 7, 9-10, 13).
Normalize the direction-finding LP with weights: norm-based weights make the choice independent of variable scaling, and an infinite weight is partial pricing (p. 8).
Return a nonbasic iterate to a basic one by a restricted LP over the free variables, with the others fixed (eq. 26, p. 8).
In a heuristic pricer for cycle-like columns, rank candidates by original cost when the duals are unreliable, since cost equals reduced cost on cycles (pp. 4, 13).
coauthors: Jean Bertrand Gauthier (first author), Jacques Desrosiers

quotes.text: In column generation, however, the primal simplex algorithm is inherently encoded in the pricing mechanism, regardless of which algorithm is actually used to reoptimize the linear restricted master programs.
Having a generic framework that conceptually hosts, for example, PS, IPS, DCA, and MMCC does not imply that we believe in a generic competitive implementation of the framework.

title: Integrating line planning, timetabling and vehicle scheduling
contribution: An integrated IP for line planning, timetabling, vehicle scheduling and passenger routing, and a GCG-based study of 75 detected Dantzig-Wolfe decompositions on one small instance showing that the canonical decomposition by planning stages is far worse than detected arrowhead structures.
problem_entry: Sequential planning makes later stages depend on earlier ones; integrating all three stages 'has not been handled before', and the integrated model is too hard to solve directly, so its structure is analysed for decomposition (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: An integrated event-activity-network IP with passenger routing, then GCG's structure detection (partial decompositions completed by other detectors, before and after presolve) to compare 75 Dantzig-Wolfe decompositions with the canonical one by planning stages (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: An IP with binaries and general integers, big-M activation and linearized products; a fixed line pool with frequency one, a periodic timetable, OD pairs routed as units on shortest paths, unlimited vehicles, one depot; a weighted-sum objective with unreported weights; one small instance whose optimum commercial solvers find (pp. 4, 6-8, 10-11).
proof_devices: Lagrangian decomposition of linking variables: one copy per block, copy equality in the master (p. 8)

Partial decompositions completed by other detectors: constraint classifiers, densities, hypergraph partitioning of the row and row-column graphs, connected components, postprocessing (pp. 9-10, Table 1)
Block and border scores as structure measures (eqs. 7-8, pp. 15-16)
Big-M activation of periodic timetabling constraints by line choice and linearized products of binaries (constraints T1-T2 and LT1, pp. 7-8)
experiments: GCG development version based on 2.1.4 with SCIP 4.0, i7-2600, 1 h per root master LP; one small instance; 75 decompositions with block and border scores, LP iterations, time and gap to the IP optimum; canonical gap 5182.32%, best 54.3%, 42 below 200% and 33 at 900% or more by my count of Table 2; no bound of the compact model reported (pp. 10-19).
positioning: Surveys sequential and two-stage integrated public transport planning, notes that most integrated approaches are heuristic and claims the three-stage integration is new; draws detection and scores from Bergner et al. 2015 and the SCIP 6.0 report (pp. 2, 9, 16).
writing: The model is introduced through a constraint-class scheme (L, P, T, V and their couplings) and a figure; three research questions as bullets; results figure by figure; an 'Outlook' instead of a conclusion, hedged ('can only be a first step') (pp. 4, 8, 12-17).
limits_future: Sized as a first step; small block and border scores only an indicator, to be confirmed by extensive computational studies; future: specialized heuristics for subproblems recognized as planning stages, robustness, stop location and crew scheduling (pp. 16-17).

method_links.note: Steps 1-5 and the checkpoint: the option space (75 decompositions) is computed on an instance small enough to know the optimum and read for surprises (canonical worst, row-column partitioning with connected components best, a middle range of block counts best, gaps split into small and huge); the proxy scores are checked against the outcomes and called 'only an indicator and no guarantee'.
Step 4: the generic solver is the measuring instrument across decompositions, before any tailored code.

Step 2 and the Limitations line: the compact model is solved by commercial solvers only to get the optimum for the gap; its bound, nodes and time are not reported, and no root bound is compared with the compact LP or a solver's root bound after cuts (Workflow B's go/no-go). The natural planning-stage structure, which the Limitations line would probe with, is the worst decomposition found (5182.32% against a minimum of 54.3%).
Step 1: one small instance and no general set; the claim is sized to it ('can only be a first step').

transferable: Before building branch-and-price for an integrated model, enumerate the decompositions a detector finds on the original and the presolved model, solve each root master LP under one limit on an instance with a known optimum, and plot the gap against the detector and against the number of blocks (pp. 10-15).
Treat the canonical decomposition by planning stages as one candidate among many, not as the default (pp. 8, 12).
Score each decomposition by its relative block area and border area, and check the scores against the measured gaps before trusting them (pp. 15-16).
Handle linking variables with one copy per block plus copy-equality rows in the master (Lagrangian decomposition) (p. 8).
coauthors: Christian Puchert, Philine Schiewe, Anita Schöbel (alphabetical author list)

quotes.text: Due to the then poor lower bound, the gap is still at 5182.32 % which is far from optimal.
Nevertheless, low block and border scores are only an indicator and no guarantee for good solvability

title: Polyhedral results on the stable set problem in graphs containing even or odd pairs
contribution: Polyhedral characterizations of odd pairs (adding the edge vw cuts STAB(G) by just the edge inequality) and even pairs (contracting vw gives the face x_v = x_w) in arbitrary graphs, with a corollary on when the edge inequalities of F on top of the stable set polytope of the rest give STAB(G).
problem_entry: From perfect graph theory: even and odd pairs, tools in the proofs of the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem, are suggested to impose structure on the stable set polytope of arbitrary graphs (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Odd pair iff STAB(G + vw) = STAB(G) with x_v + x_w ≤ 1; even pair iff STAB(G/vw) is the contracted face x_v = x_w; corollary: E ∖ F contains all odd induced cycles iff STAB(V, E ∖ F) plus the edge inequalities of F gives STAB(G) (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Simple undirected graphs, not necessarily perfect; STAB and the clique-constrained fractional polytope QSTAB (p. 2).
proof_devices: Necessity via an odd induced cycle through vw whose odd-cycle inequality separates the two sides (Theorem 1, p. 3)
Meyniel's exchange on the component of G[S1 ∪ S2] that contains v (Theorem 1, p. 3)
Induction on |F| for the edge-set version (Corollary 1, p. 3)
Contraction in place of edge addition for even pairs (Theorem 2, p. 4)
positioning: Rooted in perfect graph theory (Lovász, Fulkerson, Chvátal, Meyniel, Chudnovsky et al.) and the Perfect Graphs book co-edited by Reed; no optimization or decomposition literature cited (pp. 2, 4).
writing: A four-page short communication: an abstract that states a suggestion and the result, a one-page recap of STAB against QSTAB, then two theorems and a corollary with compact proofs (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated; neither Dantzig-Wolfe nor computation is mentioned (pp. 1-4).

method_links.note: Exit B, the theory end only: a class-level characterization with short proofs. Corollary 1 has the form of the hull condition that card S052 records as Theorem 7 of the Discrete Optimization paper (DW(G, G') = STAB(G) iff G' contains all odd induced cycles), with G' = H [inferred; S071 states no Dantzig-Wolfe link]. The computational map that Method 2 puts before the proof is absent.

transferable: Prove that the convex hull of a subproblem plus the remaining inequalities equals the full hull by an exchange on two stable sets: take the component of their union that contains v and swap its parts; extend from one edge to an edge set by induction (p. 3).
Prove the necessity of such a hull condition with a valid inequality of the full hull that the candidate description misses, here the odd-cycle inequality of an odd induced cycle (p. 3).
coauthors: Jonas T. Witt (first author), Bruce Reed (Lübbecke corresponding author)

quotes.text: We suggest that such pairs impose a lot of structure also in arbitrary, not just perfect graphs.
To this end, we adopt Meyniel’s proof technique to prove results about the stable set polytope of an arbitrary graph and an even or odd pair within it.
